1.pericope_label: The ordinance of the red heifer; Eleazar and the sprinkled blood

schools.summary: Date the ordinance to Sinai on rabbinic authority; make the killing the priest’s own office and the people’s offering vicarious; read the removal outside the camp as the sign of a curse fulfilled at Golgotha, guarded against the inference that the victim was polluted; and take the aim of the rite to be that purity can come only from the sanctuary.

Explain the law as an emergency provision against the massed defilement of the wilderness death sentence; deny that the priest killed the victim; and account for the wholly extramural rite by its purpose, which was not fellowship at the altar but an antidote to the infection of death.

Refer both the species and the colour to Egyptian cult practice that the law was framed against; and read the colour, the untouched neck and the place of burning as figures of Christ’s blood, his voluntary submission and his suffering outside the gate.

Explain the colour by its rarity and the exacting rabbinic standard, and press the typology of the red earth and the reddened Christ, while denying that the rite was properly a sacrifice of expiation since it was not performed at the altar.

debates: When the ordinance was given: at Sinai and merely repeated here (Gill, from Aben Ezra and Jewish tradition), or now, as a remedy for the unprecedented mortality following God’s sentence (Keil).
Who slew the heifer: the priest, as his peculiar office (Calvin), or a member of the congregation, the priest doing nothing but sprinkle (Keil). The two are irreconcilable.
Why the heifer was red: to counter Egyptian sacrifices to Typhon (Clarke), because the colour was rare and therefore remarkable (Henry), or to shadow the blood of Christ (Wesley, Henry).
Whether the rite was properly expiatory — Henry denies it, on the ground that it was not performed at the altar.
outliers: Clarke alone explains both the species and the colour of the victim as polemic against Egyptian religion.
Keil alone ties the law to the demographic emergency of the wilderness generation rather than to typology.
Gill alone reports the physical mechanics of the sprinkling, from Maimonides and the Targum.

5.pericope_label: The burning of the heifer; cedar, hyssop and scarlet; the ashes gathered

schools.summary: Resolve the paradox that a purifying sacrifice defiles its ministers by locating the pollution outside the victim, and read the materials cast into the fire as joining blood to water and as evidence of the victim’s own purity; preserve the rabbinic ceremonial in full and defend the rendering of the water’s name.

Explain the officiants’ defilement by the transfer of the uncleanness of sin and death to the sin-offering rather than by contact with unclean people; assign emblematic senses to cedar, hyssop and scarlet; and mark the structural seam between the general rules and the particular cases.

Draw two lessons from the priest’s defilement — the imperfection of the Levitical priesthood, and Christ reckoned a sinner for our sakes — and explain the water’s name from the separated condition of those it cleansed.

debates: Why those who handled the heifer became unclean: because they had acted for unclean people and shared their uncleanness (a view Keil names and rejects), or because the uncleanness of sin and death had passed to the sin-offering (Keil, Calvin, Gill).
Whether cedar, hyssop and scarlet carry emblematic meanings of their own (Ellicott) or were cast in for the functional purpose of joining the blood’s sprinkling to the water’s (Calvin).
Whether water of separation is named from expiation or from the separated state of the unclean — Calvin and Wesley differ on the ground of the name.
Who is meant by the stranger: the Gentile afar off who receives remission through Christ (Ellicott) or simply a proselyte (Wesley).
outliers: Gill alone applies the defilement of the ministers to the guilt of those who put Christ to death, and alone preserves the ritual detail — the tower of wood, the threefold question, the causeway over the Kidron, the sifting of the ashes.
Keil alone names and rejects a modern commentator’s explanation of the officiants’ uncleanness.

11.pericope_label: He that toucheth the dead; the third day and the seventh; the penalty of neglect

schools.summary: Read the seven-day defilement as a measure of man’s peculiar sinfulness; expound the idiom by which purifying is called sinning, and admit with the rabbis that the reason of the law is unknown; restrict the death penalty to presumptuous neglect, and find Christ’s resurrection typified in the third day.

Make the corpse a mirror of the curse and extend the defilement to the dead works of unbelief; distinguish postponed purification, which was redeemable, from entering the sanctuary unclean, which was capital; and insist the offence lay not in the touch itself but in polluting holy things.

Ground the longer defilement in death as the wages of sin; propose a construction of the verse requiring both the third and the seventh day, on the authority of the versions; and state the consequence of neglect without softening it.
Call the law one of the greatest and most unaccountable burdens of the ceremonial system, since far grosser uncleannesses were purged with common water by evening.

debates: Why a corpse defiles seven days and a carcase only one: to mark man’s peculiar sinfulness (Clarke), because death is the wages of sin (Ellicott), because every dead man shows the defacing of God’s image (Calvin) — while Henry calls the disproportion simply unaccountable.
Whether the verse requires purification on both the third and the seventh day, as Ellicott argues from the Greek and Latin versions, or admits the sense of the received rendering.
Whether the death penalty falls on every neglect or only on presumptuous neglect (Wesley) — and whether it attaches to the uncleanness itself or to entering the sanctuary in it (Calvin).
Whether the reason for a red female victim is recoverable at all — Clarke reports the rabbinic confession that it is not.
outliers: Henry alone refuses to justify the law and calls it unaccountable.
Calvin alone extends the defilement of the dead to the dead works of unbelief.
Clarke alone explains the Hebrew idiom by an English one, and alone quotes the admission that Solomon could not find the reason out.

14.pericope_label: The law of the tent and the open vessel; the water of separation prepared

schools.summary: Extend the law from tents to houses on the ground that tents were merely the present circumstance, narrow the open vessel to earthenware on rabbinic authority, cover every manner of death between the two clauses, and deny — against the Targum — that the sprinkler had to be a priest.
Correct the rendering to the ashes of the burnt sin-offering, explain the uncovered vessel by the corpse’s smell rather than by symbolism, and credit hyssop with an inherent purifying property.

Take the running water for the Spirit of God, and press the consequence: those who claim Christ’s righteousness without submitting to his Spirit deceive themselves, since the ashes cleanse only in the running water.

debates: Whether the open vessel means earthenware only (Gill, from the Targum, Jarchi and Maimonides) or any uncovered vessel (Keil, who explains the covering by the smell of the corpse).
Whether the man who sprinkled had to be a priest — asserted by the Targum of Jonathan, denied by Gill, and left open by Keil.
Whether hyssop was chosen for an inherent purifying power (Keil) or as an emblem.
outliers: Wesley alone makes the running water a figure of the Spirit and uses it against a presumed reliance on imputed righteousness.
Gill alone insists the law of the tent applies equally to a house.

19.pericope_label: The sprinkling on the third and seventh day; the perpetual statute

schools.summary: Explain why a cleansing water defiles its handler — the virtue lies in God’s appointment and not in the work done, the arrangement exposes the imperfection of the Levitical priesthood, and it proves that an ordinance does not depend on the minister’s own purity; and restrict the penalty to contemptuous refusal.

Set out the ambiguity of the Hebrew and decide it from the following clause in favour of persons infecting things; explain the closing verse as forestalling the charge that God punishes trifles with death; and limit the perpetual statute to the coming of Christ.
Repair the pronouns of the nineteenth verse so that the clean man purifies and the unclean man washes, and otherwise let the text stand.

debates: Whether the last verse means whosoever toucheth an unclean thing or whosoever the unclean person toucheth — Hebrew has no neuter, and Calvin says either sense would serve before deciding from the next clause.
Who the unclean person of the last verse is: the man defiled merely by handling the water, or the man under the seven-day uncleanness (Gill and Wesley take the second).
How a statute can be called perpetual — Gill alone bounds it at the abolition of the ceremonial law.
Whether the sprinkler had to be a priest, as the Targum of Jonathan has it.
outliers: Wesley alone confronts the paradox that the same water cleanses and defiles, and draws from it that an ordinance’s efficacy does not depend on the minister.
Calvin alone treats the closing verse as an anticipation of the reader’s objection rather than as further legislation.
